stem: A 67-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis and an irregular pulse suddenly develops right facial droop and right arm weakness. She follows commands but speaks only in halting, effortful short phrases and cannot repeat sentences. She also coughs when swallowing. She has no headache.
oneliner: 67F + rheumatic mitral stenosis, irregular pulse + sudden R face/arm weakness + halting speech with good comprehension + no headache → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Leg weakness greater than arm**, little face involvement; this case has face and arm weakness with aphasia
whyNot.B: **Visual field loss** is the main deficit; no hemianopia or limb weakness is described
whyNot.D: **No cortical signs** (aphasia, neglect) in a lacune; here language is clearly impaired
whyNot.E: **Sudden deficit without headache or vomiting** and a clear embolic source favor ischemia

answer: Middle cerebral artery stroke (left MCA embolic stroke)
why: **Face and arm weakness + aphasia** in a patient with **AF/rheumatic mitral disease** = embolus to the dominant MCA.

stem: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden weakness limited to the left hand and forearm. His leg is spared, and his speech, vision and coordination are normal.
oneliner: 62M + AF + sudden L hand and forearm weakness + leg spared + normal speech, vision, coordination → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Middle cerebral artery stroke (right MCA branch)

whyNot.B: **Leg and foot** area would be weak, not the hand
whyNot.C: **Visual field defect** would dominate; vision is normal here
whyNot.D: **Face, arm and leg are usually weak together** in a lacune; isolated hand points to a cortical branch
whyNot.E: **Coordination is normal**; weakness is cortical, not cerebellar

why: **Hand and forearm** motor cortex lies on the lateral convexity, supplied by the **MCA**; left-sided weakness means the right hemisphere.

stem: A 59-year-old smoker with hypertension wakes with left arm and leg weakness and a drooping left lower face; he can wrinkle his forehead. Reflexes on the left are brisk, tone is increased, and the left plantar response is extensor. Sensation, vision and speech are normal.
oneliner: 59M + HTN + sudden L arm/leg weakness + L lower face droop, forehead spared + brisk reflexes, upgoing toe → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Ischemic stroke (right hemisphere or internal capsule)

whyNot.A: **Forehead is spared** and limbs are weak here, so this is not an isolated peripheral facial palsy
whyNot.C: The **face is involved**; a cord lesion would spare it
whyNot.D: **Hyperreflexia, raised tone and an extensor plantar** are objective UMN signs that cannot be produced voluntarily
whyNot.E: **Spasticity, hyperreflexia and extensor plantar**, with asymmetric onset, not symmetric flaccid areflexia

why: **Sudden unilateral face, arm and leg weakness** with **spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski** and forehead sparing = upper motor neuron lesion above the pons, most likely an ischemic stroke.

stem: A 73-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension had sudden left-sided weakness 4 months ago; CT at that time showed no blood. The weakness persists with brisk reflexes and mild dysarthria. He dies of an unrelated myocardial infarction. The right deep hemisphere shows a small, sharply demarcated cavity; microscopy shows macrophages and astrocytic scar, with no hemosiderin.
oneliner: 73M + HTN + sudden L weakness 4 mo ago, CT no blood + autopsy: small deep cavity with gliosis, no hemosiderin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A healed bleed leaves **hemosiderin-laden macrophages**, and CT showed no blood
whyNot.C: **No fever, no capsule or pus**; the lesion is a scarred cavity
whyNot.D: A tumor would be **cellular and mass-forming**; this is a cavity with scar
whyNot.E: **Deficit persisted for months**, and TIAs resolve within 24 hours

why: **Abrupt deficit, CT negative for blood**, now a **cavity with gliosis and no hemosiderin** = healed ischemic infarct.

dx: Old ischemic stroke with corticospinal tract degeneration
stem: A 76-year-old man had a sudden right hemiparesis 2 years ago. Since then the right arm and leg became stiff and spastic with brisk reflexes. He dies of pneumonia. A photograph of an axial section through the midbrain at autopsy is shown.
oneliner: 76M + R hemiparesis 2 y ago → now spastic + [photo of midbrain] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Old ischemic stroke with Wallerian degeneration of the corticospinal tract

whyNot.A: **No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia**; the deficit is a spastic hemiparesis after a sudden event
whyNot.B: **No ataxia or dysmetria** is described
whyNot.C: A fresh bleed would be **hemorrhagic**; this is a chronic atrophic change
whyNot.E: **No crossed pain-temperature loss, hoarseness or dysphagia** are described

answer: Old ischemic stroke with corticospinal tract (crus cerebri) degeneration
why: **Spastic hemiparesis after a sudden event** plus **one shrunken crus cerebri** = Wallerian degeneration of corticospinal fibers from an old contralateral infarct.

image.prompt: Axial gross section through the midbrain showing the two cerebral peduncles; the one on the left of the picture is markedly shrunken and grayish-tan compared with the plump, normal-colored peduncle on the other side. Substantia nigra appears normally pigmented. No text or labels.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought in 90 minutes after sudden weakness of the left face, arm and leg while eating. He has no headache, no prior seizures, and fingerstick glucose is 98 mg/dL. The ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves.
oneliner: 72M + sudden L face/arm/leg weakness 90 min ago + no headache + glucose 98 + ECG: no P waves → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No headache**, and AF gives a clear embolic source; hemorrhage typically brings headache and vomiting
whyNot.C: **No preceding seizure** to cause postictal weakness
whyNot.D: **No headache or aura** to suggest migraine
whyNot.E: **Glucose is normal**

why: **Sudden hemiparesis** + **AF with no P waves** and normal glucose = cardioembolic ischemic stroke.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with hypertension suddenly develops weakness of the right leg, with the right face and arm relatively spared. She cannot tell the position of her right great toe with eyes closed, and the right plantar response is extensor. Her speech is normal.
oneliner: 69F + HTN + sudden R leg weakness, face/arm spared + lost toe position sense + upgoing toe → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Face and arm are weaker than leg** in MCA stroke, and aphasia would be likely
whyNot.B: **Visual field loss** would be expected; weakness is not typical
whyNot.C: Lacunes cause **equal weakness of face, arm and leg** without cortical sensory loss
whyNot.D: **Position sense is lost** and only one side is affected; anterior spinal syndrome spares dorsal columns and is bilateral

why: **Contralateral leg weakness and foot sensory loss** with face/arm sparing = medial frontoparietal cortex (leg area) supplied by the **ACA**.

stem: A 63-year-old man cannot name a key or a cup placed in front of him, yet names each at once when he handles it. Visual acuity, eye movements, speech and strength are normal.
oneliner: 63M + cannot name objects by sight, names them by touch + normal acuity, eye movements, speech, strength → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Strength is normal**; ACA strokes cause leg weakness
whyNot.B: **Speech is fluent and normal**; no aphasia or hemiparesis
whyNot.D: **No motor or sensory deficit**, which is what a lacune causes
whyNot.E: **Alert, with normal eye movements**; no coma or quadriparesis

why: **Visual agnosia** with intact touch and normal acuity = occipitotemporal association cortex, **PCA** territory.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation suddenly loses vision on the left side in both eyes, though central vision remains intact. She has no weakness, sensory loss or language difficulty.
oneliner: 70F + rheumatic MS + AF + sudden L-sided visual loss in both eyes, central vision intact + no weakness or aphasia → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No weakness, aphasia or neglect** which MCA infarcts usually bring
whyNot.B: **Macular sparing** is typical of occipital infarct; optic tract lesions are incongruous without sparing
whyNot.C: **Isolated visual field loss**, not a pure motor or sensory syndrome
whyNot.D: **Visual loss is left-sided in both eyes**, not bitemporal

why: **Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing** and an embolic source = occipital cortex infarct, **PCA** territory.

stem: A 64-year-old man with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has sudden, equal weakness of the right face, arm and leg. Sensation, vision, language and cognition are normal, and he has no neglect. CT shows no blood.
oneliner: 64M + long-standing HTN + sudden equal R face/arm/leg weakness + normal sensation, speech, vision + CT no blood → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No aphasia, neglect or visual loss**, which cortical emboli typically cause
whyNot.C: **CT shows no blood**
whyNot.D: **CT shows no blood**, and SAH causes a thunderclap headache rather than a pure hemiparesis
whyNot.E: **Abrupt onset**; tumors cause gradually progressive deficits

why: **Pure motor hemiparesis** with **no cortical signs** in a long-standing hypertensive = small-vessel **lacunar infarct** (internal capsule).

stem: A 58-year-old man with hypertension suddenly develops vertigo, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. He has lost pain and temperature sensation on the right face and the left arm and leg, and the right gag reflex is absent. He is alert, strength is normal, the tongue protrudes midline, and hearing is normal.
oneliner: 58M + HTN + sudden vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia + R face and L body pain-temperature loss + absent R gag + normal strength → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Contralateral weakness and tongue deviation** would occur; strength and tongue are normal here
whyNot.B: **Facial paralysis and hearing loss** would be expected; face moves and hearing is normal
whyNot.C: **Whole contralateral hemibody including face** would be affected; here the face is crossed with the body
whyNot.E: **Coma or quadriparesis** would be expected; he is alert with normal strength

why: **Ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain-temperature loss** with **hoarseness, dysphagia, absent gag** = lateral medulla (nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal and spinothalamic tracts), **PICA**.

stem: A 66-year-old man with diabetes suddenly has weakness of the right arm and leg, sparing the face. When he sticks out his tongue it deviates to the left. Pain and temperature sensation are normal, but vibration and position sense are reduced on the right. Eye movements are normal.
oneliner: 66M + DM + sudden R arm/leg weakness, face spared + tongue deviates L + reduced R vibration/position sense + normal eye movements → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Pain-temperature loss, hoarseness and dysphagia** would be present; pain and temperature are normal
whyNot.C: **Ipsilateral facial paralysis and hearing loss** would be expected
whyNot.D: **Quadriplegia with only vertical eye movements**; he has hemiparesis
whyNot.E: **Third nerve palsy** would be present; eye movements are normal

answer: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory)
why: **Contralateral hemiparesis** with **ipsilateral tongue deviation** and medial lemniscus loss = medullary pyramid, hypoglossal nucleus and medial lemniscus.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension suddenly has drooping of the left eyelid. The left eye is turned down and out, the left pupil is dilated and does not react, and she has weakness of the right arm and leg.
oneliner: 61F + HTN + sudden L ptosis, eye down and out, dilated pupil + R arm and leg weakness → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hoarseness, dysphagia, crossed pain-temperature loss** would be present; there is a third nerve palsy instead
whyNot.B: **Contralateral pain and sensory loss** would dominate; this patient has weakness
whyNot.C: **Finger agnosia, acalculia, agraphia, left-right confusion** would be expected
whyNot.D: **Contralateral tremor or ataxia** (red nucleus) would accompany the third nerve palsy; none here

why: **Ipsilateral third nerve palsy** + **contralateral hemiparesis** = cerebral peduncle and oculomotor fascicle in the midbrain.

stem: A 66-year-old man with severely uncontrolled hypertension (BP 230/130 mm Hg) has a sudden severe headache and vomiting while lifting. Within an hour he has right-sided weakness and then becomes comatose. There was no head injury and his neck is supple.
oneliner: 66M + BP 230/130 + sudden headache and vomiting → R hemiparesis → coma + no trauma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Focal hemiparesis** comes first, with a **supple neck**; aneurysm rupture gives thunderclap headache and meningismus
whyNot.C: Usually younger patients with **seizures** or prior bruit; this is a long-term hypertensive
whyNot.D: **No head injury**
whyNot.E: **Headache, vomiting and rapid coma** point to bleeding; ischemia usually presents without them

why: **Uncontrolled hypertension** + **sudden headache, vomiting, hemiparesis then coma** = hypertensive hemorrhage, typically in the basal ganglia.

stem: A 24-year-old man is struck on the left temple with a bat and briefly loses consciousness. He then talks normally for about 2 hours before becoming drowsy. The left pupil is now dilated and reacts poorly to light. He takes no anticoagulants.
oneliner: 24M + bat blow to L temple + brief LOC + 2 h normal → drowsy + L dilated pupil → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A **venous, slowly progressive** bleed in older or alcoholic patients; a temple blow with rapid deterioration in hours suggests arterial
whyNot.B: **Trauma preceded the problem** and there is no thunderclap headache or neck stiffness
whyNot.D: **Progressive deterioration** and a blown pupil; a concussion clears
whyNot.E: **A lucid interval** is present; contusions cause immediate focal deficits without one

why: **Temple trauma** + **lucid interval** then rapid decline with **ipsilateral blown pupil** = arterial bleed from the **middle meningeal artery**.

stem: A 9-year-old boy falls off his bicycle and hits his head. He briefly passes out, then seems normal for several hours. He is now increasingly sleepy and has weakness of the right arm and leg. A CT scan of the head is shown.
oneliner: 9M + head injury + brief LOC + lucid hours → sleepy + R hemiparesis + [CT] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The collection is **lens-shaped and stops at the sutures**, not crescent-shaped across them
whyNot.C: Blood is **outside the brain in a lens**, not filling the sulci and cisterns
whyNot.D: **Lucid interval** is present; a contusion causes immediate focal deficits
whyNot.E: The blood is **extra-axial**, not within the brain parenchyma

why: **Lucid interval** then somnolence and hemiparesis, with a **biconvex extra-axial collection** = epidural hematoma.

image.prompt: Axial non-contrast head CT showing a well-defined, biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense extra-axial collection over the left temporal convexity with mild midline shift to the right. No text or labels.

stem: An 81-year-old man with brain atrophy falls and strikes his head. He seems fine, but over the next 3 weeks becomes increasingly drowsy with headache. He now has left hemiparesis, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response.
oneliner: 81M + atrophic brain + head strike + well → 3 wk of drowsiness and headache + L hemiparesis, Babinski → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Weeks of slow progression** in an elderly patient, not a short lucid interval over hours
whyNot.B: **No thunderclap headache or neck stiffness**
whyNot.C: **Hemiparesis and drowsiness** are present, with no urinary incontinence or gait apraxia
whyNot.E: **Gradual, not sudden**, onset after trauma

why: **Minor head trauma in an atrophic elderly brain** + **delayed, progressive drowsiness and hemiparesis** = bridging vein bleed, subdural hematoma.

stem: A 74-year-old man is found unresponsive after being struck by a car as a pedestrian. He has brisk reflexes on the left. A CT scan of the head is shown.
oneliner: 74M + pedestrian struck + unresponsive + L hyperreflexia + [CT] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: The collection is **crescent-shaped and crosses suture lines**, not biconvex
whyNot.C: Blood **lies over the convexity**, not in the basal cisterns and sulci
whyNot.D: Blood is **outside the ventricles**
whyNot.E: CT would show **tiny punctate hemorrhages or be normal**, not a large collection

why: A **crescent-shaped extra-axial collection** over the convexity after trauma = acute subdural hematoma (bridging vein tear).

image.prompt: Axial non-contrast head CT showing a crescent-shaped hyperdense extra-axial blood collection along the right cerebral convexity, spreading across the hemisphere, with sulcal effacement and mild midline shift to the left. No text or labels.

stem: A 70-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in 2 days after a fall, confused and then more drowsy. The right pupil is now dilated and sluggish, and the left arm is weak. A CT scan of the head is shown.
oneliner: 70M + alcohol use + fall 2 d ago + drowsy + R dilated pupil + L arm weakness + [CT] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The collection is **crescent-shaped, not lens-shaped**, and stays over the hemisphere surface in a diffuse sheet
whyNot.B: CT would show **small punctate hemorrhages** rather than a large extra-axial collection
whyNot.C: The blood is **extra-axial**, not a parenchymal bruise
whyNot.D: The blood is **outside the brain tissue**, not within the parenchyma

why: A **crescent-shaped extra-axial collection with midline shift** and a **dilated ipsilateral pupil** with contralateral weakness = subdural hematoma with herniation.

image.prompt: Axial non-contrast head CT showing a large crescent-shaped hyperdense extra-axial collection over the right hemisphere with marked midline shift to the left and effacement of the right lateral ventricle. No text or labels.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is found pulseless on her kitchen floor by her daughter. Paramedics restart her heart after about 10 minutes of CPR. She is stuporous for several days. Two weeks later she is awake and talks fluently, with normal naming and language and no weakness. Pupils, eye movements and gag reflex are normal. She remembers her childhood well but cannot recall anything that happened after the arrest and repeatedly asks where she is. She has no fever, no known alcohol use and no prior memory problems.
oneliner: 68F + found pulseless, CPR ~10 min + stupor then awake + can't form new memories, old memories fine + normal language, eye movements + no fever → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Abrupt onset after an arrest**, with no prior months-long decline
whyNot.B: **No fever, seizures or headache**
whyNot.C: **Eye movements are normal** and she does not drink alcohol
whyNot.D: **No weakness, abulia or personality change**; memory is the main deficit

why: **Prolonged circulatory arrest** followed by **anterograde amnesia** with preserved brainstem function = hippocampal neurons lost to anoxia.

stem: A 26-year-old soldier is knocked down by a nearby explosion and loses consciousness briefly. Over the next days he has headache, poor concentration and light sensitivity. CT of the head is normal.
oneliner: 26M + blast knocks him down + brief LOC + days of headache, poor concentration, photophobia + normal CT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No focal deficit**, and symptoms are diffuse
whyNot.C: **Only brief LOC** with a normal CT; DAI causes prolonged coma
whyNot.D: **CT is normal** and he did not deteriorate after a lucid interval
whyNot.E: **No nightmares, flashbacks or avoidance** are described; LOC and post-concussive symptoms follow trauma to the head

why: **Blast head trauma** with **brief LOC** and **post-concussive symptoms** with a normal CT = mild traumatic brain injury.

stem: A 34-year-old man was found unresponsive after a heroin overdose and had a prolonged period without a pulse. Eight weeks later, his eyes open spontaneously and he has regular sleep-wake cycles. He does not follow commands, track objects or make any purposeful movement, but he grimaces and groans to pain. His pupils react to light, corneal and gag reflexes are intact, and he breathes without a ventilator. EEG shows diffuse slowing and no isoelectric periods.
oneliner: 34M + overdose with prolonged anoxia + 8 wk later eyes open, sleep-wake cycles + no commands or tracking + breathes spontaneously, brainstem reflexes intact → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Eyes open spontaneously with sleep-wake cycles**; coma has neither
whyNot.B: **No voluntary blinking or vertical eye movement** to command; locked-in patients are aware and communicate with eyes
whyNot.D: **Spontaneous breathing, intact brainstem reflexes** and non-isoelectric EEG
whyNot.E: **No command following, visual tracking or purposeful behavior**, which minimally conscious patients show intermittently

why: **Wakefulness without awareness** (sleep-wake cycles, no purposeful response) with **intact brainstem function** weeks after anoxic injury = persistent vegetative state.

stem: A 63-year-old right-handed man suddenly cannot speak normally. His speech is slow and effortful in short phrases such as "want... water... cup," and he cannot repeat sentences. He understands questions and follows complex commands and is clearly frustrated. The right lower face droops, but he can wrinkle his forehead.
oneliner: 63M, R-handed + sudden slow effortful 2-3 word speech + good comprehension, can't repeat + R lower face droop → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Comprehension is intact** and speech is nonfluent, the reverse of fluent, empty Wernicke speech
whyNot.B: **Speech is nonfluent**, not fluent
whyNot.C: **Comprehension is intact**; global aphasia loses both
whyNot.E: **Repetition is impaired**; in transcortical motor aphasia repetition is spared

why: **Nonfluent, effortful speech** with **intact comprehension** and **right lower face weakness** = dominant inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area).

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought in after sudden confusion. He speaks fluently and at a normal rate, but with made-up words and wrong words ("I put the garden on the table with my spoon car"). He cannot follow even simple commands and cannot repeat phrases. He seems unaware that his speech makes no sense. Strength is normal.
oneliner: 72M + sudden fluent speech with wrong and made-up words + cannot follow commands or repeat + unaware + normal strength → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Speech is fluent** and comprehension is poor, the reverse of Broca
whyNot.C: **Comprehension is poor**; conduction aphasia has normal comprehension
whyNot.D: **Fluent speech and no hemiparesis**; global aphasia is nonfluent with severe weakness
whyNot.E: **Repetition is impaired**; in transcortical sensory aphasia repetition is spared

why: **Fluent, meaningless speech** with **poor comprehension and repetition** = posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area).

stem: A 58-year-old woman after a stroke speaks fluently and follows complex commands, but cannot repeat the phrase "no ifs, ands or buts." She has trouble finding words when reading aloud.
oneliner: 58F + post-stroke + fluent speech + good comprehension + cannot repeat phrases → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Comprehension is good**; Wernicke is poor
whyNot.B: **Speech is fluent**, not effortful and halting
whyNot.C: **Fluent speech with intact comprehension**; global is both impaired
whyNot.D: **Repetition is impaired**; in transcortical sensory aphasia repetition is spared

why: **Fluent speech and good comprehension but poor repetition** = arcuate fasciculus lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent episodes of twitching of the right corner of the mouth and cheek lasting about a minute, with full awareness. He also has mild persistent right lower facial weakness, with the forehead spared. Speech and comprehension are normal and gaze is conjugate.
oneliner: 45M + recurrent 1-min twitching of R mouth and cheek, aware + persistent R lower face weakness, forehead spared + normal speech → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Primary motor cortex lesion (lateral precentral gyrus)

whyNot.B: **Speech is fluent and normal** here; Broca lesions cause nonfluent speech
whyNot.C: **Sensory loss** would be the main deficit; this is motor
whyNot.D: **Leg twitching or weakness** would occur; this is face
whyNot.E: **Gaze deviation** would occur; his gaze is conjugate

answer: Primary motor cortex lesion (lateral precentral gyrus)
why: **Focal motor seizure of the face** with **contralateral lower face weakness** = lateral precentral gyrus, the face area of the motor homunculus.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the left lower face, with a normal forehead. There is no limb weakness, and sensation, speech and vision are normal. She has no ear pain or recent rash, and tears and taste are normal.
oneliner: 55F + sudden L lower face weakness, forehead normal + no limb weakness + normal sensation, speech + normal tears and taste → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Forehead is spared**; Bell palsy paralyzes the whole half of the face
whyNot.C: **No crossed cranial nerve or limb signs**
whyNot.D: **No sensory loss** is present
whyNot.E: **Speech is normal**, not nonfluent

why: **Lower face weakness with forehead sparing** and **no other deficit** = upper motor neuron lesion of the contralateral precentral gyrus face area.

stem: A 66-year-old man has numbness of the right hand after a stroke. Light touch, pain, temperature and vibration are intact, but he cannot identify a coin placed in his hand with eyes closed, cannot recognize numbers traced on his palm, and has markedly impaired two-point discrimination. Strength is normal.
oneliner: 66M + post-stroke R hand numbness + cannot identify coin or traced numbers, poor 2-point discrimination + intact touch, pain, vibration + normal strength → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Strength is normal**; no motor deficit
whyNot.B: A thalamic lesion would reduce **all sensory modalities**, including pain
whyNot.D: A neuropathy would reduce **basic touch, pain and vibration**, which are intact
whyNot.E: **Vibration is intact**; dorsal column lesion would affect it

why: **Loss of graphesthesia, stereognosis and two-point discrimination** with intact basic sensation = cortical sensory loss, postcentral gyrus.

stem: A 30-year-old man hits the back of his head in a fall. Afterward his right arm is clumsy: when he reaches for his nose the finger overshoots, and fast alternating movements are slow and irregular on the right. Gait is steady, strength, reflexes and sensation are normal, and there is no vertigo.
oneliner: 30M + occipital head injury + R arm overshoots on finger-to-nose + irregular rapid alternating movements + steady gait, normal strength, no vertigo → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia**; the problem is overshoot and incoordination
whyNot.C: **Strength is normal**, so no weakness
whyNot.D: **No vertigo**, and the problem is limb overshoot, not imbalance
whyNot.E: **Gait is steady**; the vermis would cause truncal and gait ataxia while limb coordination is spared

why: **Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia** with **normal strength** = ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere.

stem: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the left parasagittal scalp. Afterward his right leg is weak, with increased tone, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, and an extensor plantar response. The arm and face are normal, sensation is intact, and bladder function is normal.
oneliner: 25M + stab wound L parasagittal scalp → R leg weakness + high tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing toe + arm, face, bladder normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Upper motor neuron lesion (left medial motor cortex)

whyNot.B: **Spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski** rather than flaccid areflexia
whyNot.C: A transection would cause **bilateral weakness, a sensory level and bladder loss**; only one leg is affected
whyNot.D: **Sensation is intact**; a hemicord lesion also causes ipsilateral position-sense loss and contralateral pain-temperature loss, and the wound is in the scalp
whyNot.E: **Bladder and sensation are normal**, and reflexes are brisk

answer: Upper motor neuron lesion (contralateral motor cortex, leg area)
why: **Contralateral leg weakness** with **spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response** = upper motor neuron lesion.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has 2 years of progressive stiffness and difficulty walking. Her legs are tight with a scissoring gait, knee jerks are brisk with sustained ankle clonus, and both plantar responses are extensor. Strength is only mildly reduced. Sensation is normal and she has no tremor.
oneliner: 48F + 2 y progressive leg stiffness, scissoring gait + brisk reflexes, clonus, bilateral upgoing toes + mild weakness + no tremor → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No tremor or bradykinesia**; the legs are spastic with brisk reflexes
whyNot.B: Gait is **scissoring and spastic with hyperreflexia**, not broad-based and ataxic
whyNot.D: **Sensation is normal** and reflexes are brisk, not reduced
whyNot.E: **Hyperreflexia and clonus** with extensor plantars, not atrophy and fasciculations

why: **Spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and bilateral extensor plantars** = upper motor neuron (corticospinal) disease.

stem: A 57-year-old man becomes suddenly unarousable and does not open his eyes to voice or pain. MRI shows infarcts in both sides of the midbrain tegmentum.
oneliner: 57M + sudden unarousable, no eye opening to pain + MRI: bilateral midbrain tegmental infarcts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: He **cannot be aroused**; narcoleptic patients wake normally
whyNot.B: He is **not aware and communicating**; locked-in patients are awake
whyNot.C: **MRI shows midbrain infarcts, not a pontine bleed**
whyNot.E: **Arousal circuitry is damaged** at the brainstem, not the cortex

why: **Sudden loss of arousal** with **bilateral midbrain tegmental lesions** = ascending reticular activating system.

stem: A 30-year-old man dives into shallow water and injures his neck. He can flex both elbows but cannot extend them, has no hand function, and cannot move his legs. All sensation is lost below the clavicles on both sides.
oneliner: 30M + diving injury + can flex elbows but not extend, no hand function, legs paralyzed + loss of all sensation below clavicles bilaterally → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Both sides** are affected equally with a sensory level, not ipsilateral weakness with crossed pain loss
whyNot.B: Weakness is **severe in the legs too** and sensation is lost completely; central cord syndrome affects the arms more than the legs
whyNot.C: The **legs and trunk sensation** are affected; a plexus injury affects one arm
whyNot.D: **All modalities** are lost, including position and vibration

answer: Cervical spinal cord injury (complete, C5-C6 level)
why: **Elbow flexion preserved (C5), extension and hand lost, paralysis and sensory loss below the clavicles** = complete cervical cord injury at about C6.

stem: A 28-year-old man has been unable to move his arms or legs since a car crash 4 months ago. He has no sensation below the shoulders, including the genitals. He gets erections when the glans is stroked, but not with erotic thoughts.
oneliner: 28M + car crash 4 mo ago + paralysis of all limbs + no sensation below shoulders + erections only with direct stroking, not thoughts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Arms are paralyzed**, and cauda equina damage would abolish reflex erection
whyNot.C: **Legs and all sensation are lost**; central cord syndrome hits the arms more than the legs and spares sacral sensation
whyNot.D: **Quadriplegia and complete sensory loss** explain it; this is not psychogenic
whyNot.E: **Both sides** are affected equally, not a one-sided hemicord pattern

why: **Quadriplegia with total sensory loss** after trauma, with **reflex erections kept but psychogenic ones lost** = complete cervical cord injury; the sacral reflex arc works but is cut off from the brain.

stem: A 21-year-old man dives into shallow water and fractures a cervical vertebra. Afterward his right arm and leg are weak, with loss of vibration and position sense on the right below the injury. Pain and temperature sensation are lost on the left side beginning a few levels below the injury.
oneliner: 21M + diving injury, cervical fracture + R arm/leg weakness + R loss of vibration/position + L loss of pain/temp → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Position and vibration are lost** on one side, so the dorsal columns are involved, unlike anterior cord syndrome
whyNot.B: **Deficits are asymmetric**, not arms-weaker-than-legs bilaterally
whyNot.D: **Weakness and pain loss** are present, not dorsal-column loss alone
whyNot.E: **One side retains** function; transection removes everything below

why: **Ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration/position** with **contralateral pain-temperature loss** = hemisection (Brown-Sequard).

stem: A 48-year-old man had a thoracic spine fracture in a car crash 6 years ago and has since had persistent loss of vibration and position sense in both legs. He has no history of syphilis, no lancinating pains, and normal vitamin B12. He dies of sepsis. A myelin-stained cross-section of the cervical cord at autopsy is shown.
oneliner: 48M + thoracic spine fracture 6 y ago + persistent loss of leg vibration/position + normal B12, no syphilis + [myelin-stained cord] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Lateral corticospinal tracts are intact** on the stain, and B12 is normal
whyNot.B: **No syphilis, lancinating pain or Argyll Robertson pupils**; pallor is limited to the midline
whyNot.C: **One fixed deficit since trauma**, no relapses; MS plaques are patchy and do not follow one tract
whyNot.E: **No central cavity** is seen and there is no dissociated sensory loss

answer: Spinal cord injury (chronic; ascending degeneration of the gracile fasciculus)
why: **Traumatic cord injury** with **loss of leg vibration and position** and **pale dorsal midline** = ascending degeneration of the fasciculus gracilis.

image.prompt: Cross-section of the cervical spinal cord stained with Luxol fast blue myelin stain: the gray matter and most white matter are stained blue, but a narrow wedge-shaped region along the dorsal midline (both gracile fasciculi) is conspicuously pale. No text or labels.

stem: A 33-year-old man had a car crash 2 years ago. He cannot move or feel his body below the nipples and does not sweat there. On a hot day his temperature climbs to 39.0 °C, while his face and neck are flushed and sweating. His blood pressure is normal and his bladder empties reflexively.
oneliner: 33M + car crash 2 y ago + paralysis, no feeling or sweating below nipples + temp 39.0 °C in heat, flushed sweating face + normal BP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Spinal cord injury (high thoracic, above sympathetic outflow)

whyNot.A: **Blood pressure is normal**; dysreflexia has paroxysmal hypertension with a noxious trigger
whyNot.C: **Two years have passed** and bladder emptying is reflexive; spinal shock is acute and flaccid
whyNot.D: **Level is at the chest**, with a reflexive bladder; cauda equina gives flaccid bladder and legs
whyNot.E: **No antipsychotic exposure** and no rigidity; the cause is loss of sweating below the cord injury

answer: Spinal cord injury (high thoracic, interrupted sympathetic outflow)
why: **Paralysis and sensory loss below the chest** with **no sweating below the lesion and overheating** = cord injury cutting the descending sympathetic control.

stem: A 44-year-old man is stabbed in the back on the right at the T8 level. Afterward he has lost pain and temperature sensation in the left leg and lower trunk, starting a few levels below the wound. Strength, vibration, position sense and reflexes are normal in both legs.
oneliner: 44M + stab wound R back T8 + L leg and trunk pain-temperature loss + normal strength, vibration, position → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Vibration and position sense are normal**
whyNot.C: **No ipsilateral weakness or proprioceptive loss**
whyNot.D: **Loss is on one side below the lesion**, not a bilateral cape-like pattern
whyNot.E: **Strength is normal** and no bilateral involvement

answer: Spinothalamic tract lesion (right lateral, contralateral deficit)
why: **Contralateral pain-temperature loss** below the lesion with everything else normal = isolated spinothalamic tract (fibers cross in the anterior white commissure).

stem: A 35-year-old man burns his hand on a stove without feeling it. Over 3 years he has lost pain and temperature sensation across both arms and upper chest, though touch and vibration are normal, and his hand muscles are wasted.
oneliner: 35M + painless burns + over 3 y cape-like pain-temperature loss over arms and chest + touch and vibration normal + hand wasting → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sensory loss is prominent**; ALS is purely motor
whyNot.B: **Gradual 3-year course** without relapses, optic neuritis or episodic deficits
whyNot.C: **Gradual, not abrupt**, onset and the legs are not bilaterally paralyzed
whyNot.E: A tumor would give **progressive long tract signs**, and the sensory loss would not be cape-like and restricted to arms and chest

why: **Cape-like pain and temperature loss** with preserved touch/vibration and **hand wasting** = central cord cavity crossing the anterior white commissure and anterior horns.

stem: A 40-year-old man was injured in a motorcycle crash 5 years ago, with a cervical cord contusion. Over the past 2 years he has developed weakness and wasting of both hands and loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms. He has no fever, no episodes of remission, and normal leg strength. MRI of the cervical spine is shown.
oneliner: 40M + cervical cord trauma 5 y ago + 2 y of hand wasting, shoulder-arm pain-temperature loss + normal legs + [MRI] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The MRI shows a **cavity within the cord**, not tonsillar descent at the foramen magnum
whyNot.B: A tumor appears as a **solid enhancing mass**, not a fluid-filled cavity
whyNot.C: Plaques are **short, patchy and relapsing**; here a long cystic cavity
whyNot.D: **Gradual over years**, not abrupt infarction

why: **Cape-like pain-temperature loss** and **hand wasting** after cord trauma, with a **fluid cavity in the cord** = post-traumatic syringomyelia.

image.prompt: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the cervical spine showing a long, smooth, fluid-bright cavity running within the center of the cervical spinal cord with mild cord expansion. The cerebellar tonsils sit normally above the foramen magnum. No text or labels.

stem: A 31-year-old scuba diver ascends rapidly from 40 meters without decompression stops. Within an hour he has back pain, loss of vibration and position sense in both legs, and an unsteady gait. Pain and temperature sensation and leg strength are normal. He has no cerebral symptoms.
oneliner: 31M + rapid scuba ascent without stops + back pain, loss of vibration and position in legs within 1 h + normal pain-temp and strength → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Dorsal columns are affected** while pain-temperature and strength are normal
whyNot.C: **Loss is bilateral**, with no hemicord pattern
whyNot.D: **No cape-like pain-temperature loss** or hand wasting
whyNot.E: **No cerebral symptoms** such as aphasia, hemiparesis or confusion

why: **Rapid ascent** + **dorsal column deficits** from nitrogen bubbles in the thoracic cord = decompression sickness.

stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has sudden horizontal double vision that is worse on looking to the right. The right eye cannot abduct. There is no ptosis, the pupils are equal and reactive, and all other eye movements are normal.
oneliner: 58M + DM + HTN + sudden horizontal diplopia worse on R gaze + R eye cannot abduct + no ptosis, pupils normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No ptosis, no dilated pupil, adduction is normal**
whyNot.B: **Double vision is horizontal**, not vertical on downward gaze
whyNot.D: **No ptosis**, and this is a sudden fixed single-muscle palsy rather than fatigable weakness
whyNot.E: **Adduction is intact**; INO would cause failure of adduction

why: **Failure of abduction** with horizontal diplopia in a diabetic = microvascular **cranial nerve VI** palsy (lateral rectus).

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a sudden severe headache and drooping of the right upper eyelid. The right eye is turned down and out and cannot move up, in or down. The right pupil is larger than the left and reacts poorly to light.
oneliner: 52F + sudden severe headache + R ptosis + R eye down and out + R pupil large and sluggish → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Eye is deviated out** with ptosis and dilated pupil; abducens palsy turns the eye in
whyNot.C: **Pupil and ptosis** are affected; trochlear palsy causes only vertical diplopia
whyNot.D: The pupil is **large** here; Horner gives miosis
whyNot.E: **The eye cannot move** and ptosis is present; optic nerve injury affects vision

why: **Ptosis, eye down and out, and a dilated pupil** = CN III palsy involving the parasympathetic fibers, as with an aneurysm compressing the nerve.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a larger left pupil. Light shone into either eye constricts the right pupil but never the left.
oneliner: 40M + L pupil larger + light in either eye → R pupil constricts, L never does → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Light in the left eye still constricts the right pupil**, so the left afferent pathway works
whyNot.B: **Right pupil responds from either eye**, so input is intact
whyNot.C: A pretectal lesion would affect **both pupils** to light
whyNot.E: The left pupil is **larger** here; Horner pupil is small

why: **One pupil never constricts** with light in either eye while the other always does = efferent (parasympathetic) defect on that side.

stem: A 50-year-old man has no blink in either eye when the left cornea is touched. Touching the right cornea makes both eyes blink.
oneliner: 50M + touch L cornea → no blink in either eye + touch R cornea → both blink → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Stimulating the left cornea would make the **right eye blink** if the left facial nerve alone were out; neither blinks here
whyNot.B: **Blinking depends on sensation and facial movement**, not the eye muscles of the oculomotor
whyNot.C: **Vision is not required** for the corneal reflex
whyNot.D: **Lateral rectus** function is not involved in blinking

why: **Absent blink from one cornea only**, with both eyes blinking from the other = afferent (V1) loss, since the facial efferent is intact.

stem: After a deep laceration across the left cheek in a car crash, a 27-year-old woman spills drinks from the corner of her mouth. A photograph of her attempting to whistle is shown.
oneliner: 27F + deep L cheek laceration + spills drinks → [photo of attempted whistle] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Sensory loss** would be the main problem; this is motor weakness of the lips
whyNot.C: Bell palsy is **idiopathic**, but this followed a **clear facial laceration**
whyNot.D: **Hoarseness and palate deviation** would be seen
whyNot.E: The **tongue** is not the problem; she cannot purse her lips

why: **Cannot purse lips or hold fluid** after cheek trauma = orbicularis oris and buccinator weakness from facial nerve branch injury.

image.prompt: Close-up photograph of a young woman's face while she tries to whistle: the left side of the lips fails to purse and the mouth is pulled toward the right, with a visible scar across the left cheek. No text or labels.

stem: A 62-year-old man has a hoarse voice and trouble swallowing. When he says "ah," the left soft palate droops and the uvula deviates to the right; the left gag response is reduced. Tongue protrusion and shoulder shrug are normal.
oneliner: 62M + hoarse voice + dysphagia + L palate droops, uvula to R on "ah" + reduced L gag + normal tongue and shrug → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hoarseness and palatal weakness** point to the vagus; isolated glossopharyngeal lesions affect taste and sensation of the posterior tongue and pharynx
whyNot.B: **Tongue protrusion is normal**
whyNot.D: **Palate and voice are affected**, not facial expression
whyNot.E: **Shoulder shrug is normal**

why: **Hoarseness, dysphagia and palatal droop with uvula pulled away** = vagus nerve (nucleus ambiguus) lesion.

dx: Orbital floor fracture with infraorbital nerve injury
stem: A 30-year-old man is punched in the left eye. He has a numb left cheek and upper lip and cannot look up fully with the left eye.
oneliner: 30M + punched in L eye + numb L cheek and upper lip + limited upgaze → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Orbital floor fracture with infraorbital nerve injury

whyNot.A: **Numbness is over the cheek and upper lip**, not the lower lip and chin
whyNot.C: **Sensory loss** with limited upgaze; facial nerve injury causes weakness, not numbness
whyNot.D: **Numbness is constant after trauma**, not episodic shocks
whyNot.E: **Limited upgaze** points to the orbital floor; arch fractures do not trap eye movement

answer: Orbital floor (blowout) fracture with infraorbital nerve injury
why: **Eye trauma** with **cheek and upper-lip numbness** = orbital floor fracture injuring the infraorbital nerve (V2).

stem: A 66-year-old smoker with weight loss and right shoulder pain has a drooping right upper eyelid, a small right pupil that dilates slowly in the dark, and no sweating on the right side of the face. He also has a hoarse voice. Eye movements are full.
oneliner: 66M + smoker, weight loss, R shoulder pain + R ptosis, small pupil, no facial sweating + hoarse voice + full eye movements → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The pupil is **small** and eye movements are full; CN III palsy gives a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye
whyNot.B: **No severe unilateral periorbital pain or tearing attacks**
whyNot.C: **Smoker with weight loss, shoulder pain and hoarseness** points to an apical lung tumor, not a cord cavity
whyNot.D: **Ptosis and anhidrosis** are present; Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral and lack ptosis

why: **Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis** in a **smoker with weight loss, shoulder pain and hoarseness** = Horner syndrome from an apical lung (Pancoast) tumor.

stem: A 40-year-old man's wife notices that his left pupil is smaller than the right. The small pupil dilates slowly in the dark, and the left upper lid droops slightly.
oneliner: 40M + L pupil smaller + dilates slowly in the dark + slight L ptosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pupil is unilateral and ptosis is present**; Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral
whyNot.B: The pupil is **small**, and the eye is not deviated
whyNot.D: An optic tract lesion **does not change pupil size**
whyNot.E: **Ptosis and dilation lag** are present; physiologic anisocoria has none

why: **Unilateral miosis with mild ptosis** and delayed dilation in the dark = interrupted sympathetic supply.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and a prior MI suddenly loses vision in the right eye without pain or headache; an hour later it has not returned. The retina is pale, with narrowed arteries.
oneliner: 68M + DM, HTN, prior MI + sudden painless R monocular vision loss, still gone at 1 h + no headache + pale retina, narrowed arteries → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The retina is **pale**, not covered by flame hemorrhages
whyNot.B: **Retina is pale with narrow arteries**, not elevated and folded
whyNot.C: Vision loss is **persistent** with a pale retina, not transient
whyNot.E: **No headache**; and the vascular risk profile favors embolism

why: **Sudden painless monocular vision loss** with a **pale retina and narrowed arteries** = retinal artery occlusion.

stem: A 5-month-old boy has had one eye that turns inward much of the time since early infancy. The red reflex is symmetric and bright in both eyes.
oneliner: 5M + one eye turns inward since early infancy + symmetric bright red reflex → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Symmetric bright red reflex**, no lens opacity
whyNot.B: **No white pupillary reflex** (leukocoria)
whyNot.D: **No tearing, photophobia or enlarged cornea**
whyNot.E: **Presents with night blindness later**, does not cause an eye to turn in infancy

why: **Eye turning in with a normal red reflex** = misaligned eyes (strabismus), with a risk of amblyopia if not corrected.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had muffled hearing in the right ear for 2 weeks after cleaning it with cotton swabs. The right ear canal is full of dark brown debris. A tuning fork on the forehead is heard louder in the right ear, and at the right mastoid it is heard longer than when held beside the ear.
oneliner: 58M + muffled right hearing after cotton swabs + canal full of debris + Weber to the right + bone > air on the right → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Weber would go to the good ear** and air > bone would be kept
whyNot.B: **Bilateral high-frequency loss** with air > bone; this is one-sided with a blocked canal
whyNot.C: **No vertigo, tinnitus or fluctuating loss**; bone > air is not seen
whyNot.D: **Gives sensorineural loss** (air > bone); the canal here is blocked

why: **Weber toward the affected ear** and **bone > air (negative Rinne)** with a wax-filled canal = conductive loss.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has slowly worsening hearing in both ears over 15 years, with little help from hearing aids. The ear canals and drums are normal and air conduction exceeds bone conduction on both sides.
oneliner: 74F + slowly worse hearing both ears 15 y + normal drums + air > bone both sides → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Air > bone** on both sides, not bone > air
whyNot.C: **Bone > air** and usually starts at 20–40 years
whyNot.D: **Symmetric in both ears**; no one-sided loss, tinnitus or imbalance
whyNot.E: **Canals are clear**

why: **Air > bone with normal canals and drums**, symmetric and slowly progressive in old age = hair cell loss (sensorineural).

stem: A 2-year-old girl has never babbled or startled to loud sounds. Her drums are normal, tympanometry is normal, and otoacoustic emissions are absent in both ears.
oneliner: 2F + no babbling or startle to sound + normal drums and tympanometry + absent otoacoustic emissions both ears → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Normal drums and tympanometry**, middle ear is fine
whyNot.C: **Otoacoustic emissions would be present** (hair cells intact)
whyNot.D: **Normal tympanometry**, no effusion
whyNot.E: **Does not occur in toddlers**, and is conductive

why: **Absent otoacoustic emissions with normal middle ear** = cochlear hair cell (sensorineural) deafness.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who works as a sewing machine operator wakes at night with numbness of the right hand, which eases when she shakes it. She has reduced sensation over the thumb, index and middle fingers and weak thumb abduction. She has no neck pain, and neck movement does not change her symptoms.
oneliner: 45F + sewing machine work + night hand numbness relieved by shaking + thumb–index–middle numbness + weak thumb abduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Little finger and ring finger are spared**; thumb abduction is median
whyNot.C: **No neck pain** and neck movement does not provoke it
whyNot.D: **Numbness is in the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers** with weak thumb abduction; radial injury gives wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness
whyNot.E: **Deficit is limited to median territory**; TOS causes medial (C8–T1) arm symptoms

why: **Night numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers with weak thumb abduction** in repetitive hand work = median nerve compression at the wrist.

stem: A 42-year-old man has had neck pain for 5 days that shoots down the back of the arm into the middle finger. Elbow extension is weak and the triceps reflex is reduced. The biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are normal and wrist extension is strong.
oneliner: 42M + neck pain down back of arm to middle finger + weak elbow extension + low triceps reflex + normal biceps reflex → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Neck pain and middle finger numbness**; wrist extension is normal
whyNot.B: **Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes normal**, thumb not involved
whyNot.C: **Little finger and hand intrinsics spared**
whyNot.E: **No thenar weakness** and the pain starts in the neck

why: **Weak triceps with low triceps reflex and middle finger pain from the neck** = C7 root.

stem: A 51-year-old woman has had 3 months of neck pain and trouble buttoning her blouse. She has numbness of the little finger and medial forearm, weak finger flexion, finger abduction and thumb abduction, and wasted hand muscles. Extending and turning her neck brings on the arm symptoms, and her radial pulses are normal.
oneliner: 51F + neck pain 3 mo + trouble with buttons + numb little finger and medial forearm + weak finger and thumb abduction + neck extension reproduces it → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Medial forearm numbness and weak thumb abduction** lie outside ulnar territory
whyNot.B: **Little finger numb** and neck movement reproduces it
whyNot.D: **Wrist and finger extension spared**; hand intrinsics are the problem
whyNot.E: **Provoked by neck extension, not arm elevation**; pulses normal

why: **Neck-provoked symptoms with deficits across ulnar and median hand muscles and the medial forearm** = lower cervical root (C8–T1).

stem: A 67-year-old man has had 3 weeks of back pain that radiates from the front of the right thigh across the knee to the inner lower leg. The knee jerk is reduced, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion are weak, and extending the spine makes the pain worse. Imaging shows an osteophyte narrowing the right L4–L5 foramen.
oneliner: 67M + back pain to anterior thigh, knee and inner leg + low knee jerk + weak knee extension and dorsiflexion + L4–L5 foraminal osteophyte → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pure lateral thigh sensory loss**, no weakness or reflex change
whyNot.B: **Ankle dorsiflexion would be normal** and there is no back pain
whyNot.C: **Knee jerk is spared** and pain runs down the lateral leg
whyNot.D: **Sensory only**; no quadriceps or dorsiflexion weakness

why: **Anterior thigh to medial leg pain with weak quadriceps and dorsiflexion, low knee jerk and L4–L5 foraminal narrowing** = L4 root.

stem: A 38-year-old warehouse worker has had low back pain for 10 days that runs down the buttock, back of the thigh and calf to the outer edge of the foot. His ankle jerk is absent and he cannot rise onto his toes on the right. Bladder function and perineal sensation are normal.
oneliner: 38M + back pain down buttock, thigh, calf to outer foot + absent ankle jerk + cannot toe-stand + normal bladder and perineal sensation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Ankle jerk is lost and plantarflexion weak**; L5 gives weak great-toe extension
whyNot.C: **Normal bladder and perineal sensation**, one side only
whyNot.D: **Plantarflexion and ankle jerk are lost**, which spare peroneal lesions
whyNot.E: **Reflex loss and plantarflexion weakness** are not seen

why: **Pain down the posterior leg to the lateral foot, absent ankle jerk and weak plantarflexion** = S1 root.

dx: Erb palsy (upper trunk brachial plexus injury)
stem: A 24-year-old man is thrown from his motorcycle and lands on his right shoulder with his head forced sideways away from it. He cannot lift the right arm, grip strength is normal, and radiographs show no fracture. A photograph of his arm at rest is shown.
oneliner: 24M + motorcycle crash, head forced away from shoulder + cannot lift arm + normal grip + no fracture + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Grip would be weak with a claw hand**; grip is normal
whyNot.B: **Would show wrist drop**, not a limp adducted arm
whyNot.D: Axillary injury weakens only shoulder abduction; it would not cause the **extended, pronated, internally rotated arm** shown
whyNot.E: **Would not cause pronated, internally rotated limp arm**

answer: Erb palsy (upper trunk brachial plexus injury)
why: **Neck forced away from shoulder, hanging adducted, internally rotated, pronated arm ('waiter's tip') with normal grip** = C5–C6 upper trunk injury.

image.prompt: A standing adult man seen from the front with the right arm hanging limp at his side, the shoulder rotated inward, the elbow straight and the forearm turned so the palm faces backward and the hand is slightly open, like a waiter taking a tip. The left arm is relaxed and normal. No text or labels.

stem: A 4.2-kg boy is born vaginally after a prolonged delivery with shoulder dystocia. The right arm lies straight at his side, turned inward with the forearm pronated, and he does not flex the elbow or abduct the shoulder on that side. The arm is not swollen or tender. His hand grasp is present, the right Moro response is absent, and a clavicle radiograph is normal.
oneliner: Newborn 4.2 kg boy + shoulder dystocia + right arm limp, adducted, internally rotated + grasp present + normal clavicle x-ray → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hand grasp is present**; Klumpke gives a weak hand
whyNot.B: **Clavicle x-ray is normal** and the arm is not tender
whyNot.D: **No swelling or tenderness** of the arm, and the posture is the classic waiter's tip with intact grasp
whyNot.E: **Elbow flexion is also lost**, not just shoulder abduction

answer: Erb palsy (upper trunk brachial plexus injury)
why: **Large baby with shoulder dystocia, adducted internally rotated pronated arm, intact grasp, normal clavicle** = C5–C6 upper trunk injury.

stem: A 29-year-old man falls from his bicycle onto his right shoulder and has a fractured right clavicle. He has weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, and numbness over the lateral shoulder and lateral forearm. Grip strength is normal and neck movement is painless.
oneliner: 29M + bike fall + right clavicle fracture + weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion + low biceps and brachioradialis reflexes + lateral shoulder and forearm numbness → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Grip is normal**; lower trunk gives weak hand and medial arm numbness
whyNot.B: **Elbow flexion and biceps reflex are also affected**
whyNot.C: **Neck movement is painless** and the injury follows direct shoulder trauma
whyNot.D: **Reflexes are reduced and sensation is lost**, which a tendon tear would not cause

why: **Shoulder trauma with weak abduction and elbow flexion, low biceps reflex and lateral shoulder/forearm numbness** = C5–C6 upper trunk.

stem: A 27-year-old man has a stab wound in the right axilla. He has numbness along the lateral forearm and an absent biceps reflex, but shoulder abduction is normal.
oneliner: 27M + stab wound to axilla + lateral forearm numbness + absent biceps reflex + normal shoulder abduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Shoulder abduction is normal**; lateral forearm is not its territory
whyNot.C: **No thumb opposition or palm/finger numbness** is described
whyNot.D: **No wrist drop or dorsal hand numbness**
whyNot.E: **Shoulder abduction is intact**, so not C5–C6 trunk

why: **Axillary wound with lateral forearm numbness and absent biceps reflex** = musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, brachialis, lateral antebrachial cutaneous).

stem: A 62-year-old man has used crutches with ill-fitting top pads for 4 weeks after a knee operation. He now has a dropped wrist, cannot extend his fingers or elbow, and has numbness over the back of the hand. Shoulder abduction is normal and the lateral shoulder has normal sensation.
oneliner: 62M + crutches 4 wk, pads in axilla + wrist drop + cannot extend fingers or elbow + dorsal hand numbness + normal shoulder abduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Shoulder abduction and lateral shoulder sensation are normal**
whyNot.B: **Wrist and finger extension fail**, not thumb opposition or finger flexion
whyNot.C: **No finger-spreading weakness or little-finger numbness**; the wrist drops
whyNot.E: **Shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are intact**

why: **Axillary pressure from crutches with wrist drop, weak finger and elbow extension and dorsal hand numbness** = radial nerve (posterior cord).

stem: A 36-year-old man has cycled about 5 hours a day for a week on a road bike. He now has painless weakness of finger spreading and cannot hold a sheet of paper between thumb and index finger without bending the thumb tip. Sensation is normal over the whole hand, including the back of the ulnar side, and thumb abduction is strong.
oneliner: 36M + cycling 5 h/day + painless weak finger spread + Froment sign + normal hand sensation + strong thumb abduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist (Guyon canal)

whyNot.B: **Thumb abduction is strong** and the median fingers are not numb
whyNot.C: **Thumb opposition and abduction are intact**
whyNot.D: **No arm or neck symptoms or sensory loss**; purely motor hand deficit
whyNot.E: **No neck pain or sensory loss**, thumb abduction normal

answer: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist (Guyon canal)
why: **Handlebar pressure, weak finger abduction, Froment sign and spared sensation** = deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve at the wrist.

stem: A 14-year-old boy falls on his outstretched arm and has a posterior elbow dislocation, which is reduced in the emergency department. Afterwards he has tingling of the ring and little fingers and cannot spread his fingers. Thumb abduction, wrist extension, finger extension and sensation over the thumb and index finger are normal.
oneliner: 14M + elbow dislocation + tingling ring and little fingers + cannot spread fingers + normal wrist extension and thumb/index sensation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Thumb and index sensation are normal**
whyNot.B: **Wrist and finger extension are normal**
whyNot.C: **Direct elbow trauma** right before onset, and thumb abduction (T1) is strong
whyNot.D: **Thumb abduction is strong**, and the injury is at the elbow

why: **Elbow trauma with ring and little finger tingling and lost finger abduction** = ulnar nerve.

stem: A 58-year-old man had a medial elbow fracture years ago and now has a claw-like ring and little finger with wasting between the metacarpals and numbness of the little finger. Thumb abduction and medial forearm sensation are normal.
oneliner: 58M + old medial elbow fracture + clawed ring and little fingers + interosseous wasting + numb little finger + normal thumb abduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No wrist drop**; the claw hand and little-finger numbness are ulnar
whyNot.B: **Thumb abduction is normal** and the index–middle fingers are not numb
whyNot.D: **Thumb abduction and medial forearm sensation are normal**
whyNot.E: **Medial forearm sensation spared** and no neck pain

why: **Claw ring/little fingers, interosseous wasting and little-finger numbness after medial elbow trauma** = ulnar nerve.

stem: A 55-year-old man cannot extend his knee after a deep wound in the upper thigh just below the inguinal ligament. The inner lower leg is numb, but hip flexion, knee flexion and thigh adduction are normal.
oneliner: 55M + deep wound below inguinal ligament + cannot extend knee + numb inner lower leg + normal hip flexion, knee flexion and adduction → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Thigh adduction is normal** and knee extension is lost
whyNot.B: **Knee extension is lost**; peroneal injury gives foot drop and lateral leg numbness
whyNot.C: **Thigh adduction is normal** and a thigh wound explains it; an L4 root lesion would also weaken adduction
whyNot.E: **Knee flexion is normal** and the numbness is medial, not lateral/posterior

why: **Lost knee extension with medial leg numbness (saphenous) and spared hip flexion/adduction** = femoral nerve below the inguinal ligament.

stem: A 22-year-old soccer player is kicked on the outer side of the right knee and has a fracture of the neck of the fibula. He now has foot drop, cannot evert the foot, and has numbness over the lateral leg and top of the foot. Plantar flexion, foot inversion and the ankle jerk are normal.
oneliner: 22M + kick to lateral knee + fibular neck fracture + foot drop + lost eversion + numb lateral leg and dorsum of foot + normal plantar flexion, inversion and ankle jerk → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Plantar flexion and ankle jerk are normal**
whyNot.C: **Plantar flexion and ankle jerk intact**, so tibial part works
whyNot.D: **Foot inversion is strong** and there is no back pain
whyNot.E: **Eversion and lateral leg sensation would be spared**

why: **Fibular neck fracture with foot drop, lost eversion and lateral leg numbness, spared plantar flexion** = common peroneal nerve.

stem: A 30-year-old man has a deep laceration over the front of the upper shin. He now has weak foot and toe dorsiflexion but can evert the foot normally, and the only numb area is the skin between the great and second toes. Plantar flexion is strong and the sole feels normal.
oneliner: 30M + deep laceration front of upper shin + weak foot/toe dorsiflexion + normal eversion + numb only between great and second toes + strong plantar flexion → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Eversion is normal and dorsiflexion is weak**, the reverse of this nerve
whyNot.B: **Eversion and lateral leg sensation would be lost**
whyNot.C: **Plantar flexion is strong**, so the tibial part works, and sensory loss is only the first web space
whyNot.D: **Plantar flexion is strong and the sole feels normal**

why: **Dorsiflexion weakness with intact eversion and numbness only in the first web space** = deep peroneal branch.

stem: A 35-year-old man who cycles 3 hours daily has penile and perineal numbness after rides, with new difficulty maintaining an erection. He has no groin pain or upper thigh numbness; gluteal and leg strength, bladder function and the cremasteric reflex are normal.
oneliner: 35M + cycles 3 h/day + penile and perineal numbness + erectile difficulty + no groin or thigh numbness + normal glutes, legs, bladder, cremasteric reflex → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No groin pain or upper thigh numbness**
whyNot.B: **Cremasteric reflex is normal** and the thigh is not numb
whyNot.C: **Gluteal strength is normal**; this nerve is motor only
whyNot.E: **Leg strength and bladder function are normal**

why: **Prolonged saddle pressure with perineal/penile numbness and erectile difficulty** = pudendal nerve compression.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a glass laceration that cut his median nerve at the wrist. Ten days later, a biopsy of the nerve segment beyond the cut shows fragmented axons, myelin debris being cleared by macrophages, and rows of proliferating Schwann cells inside intact tubes.
oneliner: 25M + median nerve cut at wrist + 10 d later: distal axons fragmented, myelin cleared by macrophages, Schwann cells in rows → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Axons would be intact** with focal myelin loss
whyNot.C: **No axon breakdown** and function returns in days to weeks
whyNot.D: **A cell body change** (swollen soma, displaced nucleus), not a distal axon change
whyNot.E: **Disorganized tangled axons at the cut end**, not distal tube degeneration

why: **Fragmented distal axons, macrophage clearance and Schwann cell tubes after a cut** = Wallerian degeneration, the path that guides regrowth.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a numb patch of skin beside her lower abdominal surgical scar, where a retractor stretched a small cutaneous nerve. Over the following months, the numb area slowly shrinks from its edge at roughly 1 mm a day, and tapping along the skin moves a tingling sensation outward. There is no pain, swelling or color change.
oneliner: 33F + numb skin beside surgical scar after retractor stretch + numb area shrinking ~1 mm/day + tapping gives advancing tingling + no pain or swelling → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Recovers within days to weeks** with no axon loss, no advancing Tinel sign
whyNot.B: **Complete transection does not recover spontaneously**; here sensation returns
whyNot.C: **Would be a painful, fixed lump**; here the numb area is shrinking
whyNot.D: **No pain, swelling or color change**

why: **Slow ~1 mm/day recovery with an advancing Tinel sign** = axon loss with intact supporting tubes (axonotmesis); axons regrow at the speed of slow axonal transport.

stem: A 35-year-old man had a lacerated forearm neurovascular bundle repaired 14 months ago and has regained his strength and sensation. A biopsy of a forearm muscle now shows large clusters of fibers of one type, replacing the normal checkerboard mix of fiber types. There is no fiber necrosis, fibrosis or inflammation.
oneliner: 35M + forearm nerve repaired 14 mo ago, strength and sensation recovered + biopsy: clusters of same fiber type instead of checkerboard + no necrosis or inflammation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Reinnervation after nerve injury (fiber type grouping)

whyNot.A: **No necrosis or fibrosis**, and strength is normal
whyNot.B: **Strength has recovered**; atrophy gives small angular fibers
whyNot.D: **No inflammatory infiltrate**
whyNot.E: **Muscle is working normally**; disuse would shrink type II fibers, not group them

answer: Reinnervation after peripheral nerve injury (fiber type grouping)
why: **Same-type fiber clusters in recovered muscle after nerve repair** = surviving motor neurons took over neighbouring fibers and converted them to their own type.

stem: A 40-year-old carpenter had his left index finger cut off at the base and reattached 6 months ago. The fingertip is still numb to light touch but is slowly improving, and tapping over the finger base gives tingling that spreads toward the tip. There is no pain, swelling or color change, the other fingers feel normal, and he has no night symptoms.
oneliner: 40M + index finger reattached 6 mo ago + numb tip slowly improving + tapping at base gives tingling toward tip + other fingers normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Other median fingers and night symptoms are normal**
whyNot.C: **Index finger is not ulnar territory** and the ring and little fingers are normal
whyNot.D: **No pain, swelling or skin temperature change**
whyNot.E: **No color change**, and the numbness started with the injury

answer: Peripheral nerve injury (digital nerve transection, regenerating)
why: **Reattached finger with numb tip that is slowly recovering and a distally advancing Tinel sign** = regenerating digital nerve.

stem: A 54-year-old man had a below-knee amputation 4 months ago and now has episodes of shooting pain lasting seconds to minutes in the foot that is no longer there, worse when he is anxious or the weather turns cold. The stump is nontender, not red, and tapping it does not trigger the pain; he is afebrile.
oneliner: 54M + below-knee amputation 4 mo ago + shooting pain in the missing foot for seconds to minutes + worse with anxiety or cold + stump nontender and afebrile → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Stump tapping does not trigger pain**
whyNot.B: **Pain is felt in the missing foot**, not in a dermatome of the remaining body
whyNot.D: **Pain is not diffuse** and is localized to the missing limb
whyNot.E: **Stump is not red or tender and no fever**

why: **Episodic shooting pain felt in the absent limb with a normal stump** = phantom limb pain.

stem: A 58-year-old man has 8 months of progressive weakness that began in the right hand and spread to both legs, with muscle cramps and trouble swallowing. He has wasting and visible twitching of the tongue and hand muscles, brisk knee jerks and an extensor plantar response. Sensation is normal.
oneliner: 58M + 8 mo progressive weakness hand then legs + trouble swallowing + tongue and hand wasting with twitching + brisk reflexes + extensor plantar + normal sensation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No fatigable weakness**; there is wasting, twitching and brisk reflexes
whyNot.B: **No sensory loss, optic or relapsing episodes**; has muscle wasting with twitching
whyNot.C: **Progresses over months with brisk reflexes**, not days with areflexia
whyNot.D: **Upper motor neuron signs are present** (brisk reflexes, extensor plantar)

why: **Progressive weakness with fasciculations and wasting plus brisk reflexes and Babinski, sensation normal** = upper and lower motor neuron disease.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has had 9 months of progressive weakness and wasting of both hands, with twitching of her hands, trapezius and tongue. Sensation is normal. Nerve conduction studies are normal with no conduction block, and EMG shows active denervation in the cervical, thoracic and bulbar regions. MRI of the cervical spine shows no cord compression.
oneliner: 60F + 9 mo hand weakness and wasting + twitching of hands, trapezius, tongue + normal sensation + no conduction block + EMG denervation in 3 regions + no cord compression → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No cord compression on MRI** and bulbar muscles are involved
whyNot.B: **No conduction block** and denervation spreads to bulbar regions
whyNot.C: **Fasciculations with neurogenic EMG denervation**, not a myopathic pattern
whyNot.E: **Wasting and fasciculations with EMG denervation**, not fatigable weakness

why: **Hand wasting with fasciculations, normal sensation, no conduction block and EMG denervation in several regions with no compression** = ALS.

stem: A 31-year-old man has 3 days of tingling and weakness that began in both feet and has climbed to the thighs. He had diarrhea 2 weeks ago. Weakness is symmetric, knee and ankle reflexes are absent, there is no sensory level, and bladder function is normal.
oneliner: 31M + diarrhea 2 wk ago + 3 d ascending symmetric leg weakness and tingling + absent reflexes + no sensory level → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Reflexes are absent**, not normal, and weakness follows an organic pattern
whyNot.C: **Symmetric with tingling**; polio is asymmetric without sensory symptoms
whyNot.D: **Reflexes are absent** and weakness is not fatigable or ocular
whyNot.E: **No sensory level or bladder involvement**, reflexes are absent

why: **Ascending symmetric weakness with absent reflexes after diarrhea** = acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.

stem: A 44-year-old man has had 6 days of ascending numbness and unsteady walking after a respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. He has mild distal leg weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes, and loss of vibration and joint position sense in the feet. His gait is wide-based and worse with his eyes closed. There is no sensory level, his bladder works normally, his pupils react normally, and he does not drink alcohol.
oneliner: 44M + resp infection 2 wk ago + 6 d ascending numbness + absent reflexes + lost vibration and position sense + ataxic gait + no sensory level, normal pupils and bladder → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No sensory level or bladder involvement**, and reflexes are absent, not brisk
whyNot.B: **Developed in days, normal pupils, no lightning pains**
whyNot.C: **Evolves over days, not months**, with absent reflexes
whyNot.E: **He does not drink alcohol** and onset is days after an infection

why: **Days of ascending sensory loss with areflexia after an infection and no sensory level** = acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.

stem: A 59-year-old man has had poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 15 years. He has wasting between the metacarpals of his right hand with difficulty spreading the fingers, and he cannot stand on the toes of his left foot. Pinprick sensation is reduced over both feet. He has no fever, weight loss, rash or hypertension, and he drinks no alcohol.
oneliner: 59M + T2DM poorly controlled 15 y + hand interosseous wasting with weak finger spread + cannot toe-stand on left + stocking pinprick loss + no fever, rash or alcohol → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Interossei (ulnar) are wasted, not thenar**, and plantar flexion loss is not explained
whyNot.B: **Drinks no alcohol**
whyNot.D: **Hand and foot deficits in different nerves**, one root cannot explain both
whyNot.E: **No fever, weight loss, rash or hypertension**

why: **Long poorly controlled diabetes with separate ulnar (interossei) and tibial (plantar flexion) nerve deficits plus stocking sensory loss** = diabetic neuropathy.

stem: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years has burning pain in both feet. Even the touch of bed sheets is painful. Strength, vibration sense and ankle reflexes are normal, but pinprick is reduced over the feet. Pulses are strong, he drinks no alcohol, and his vitamin B12 level is normal.
oneliner: 55M + T2DM 12 y + burning feet + pain from bed sheets + reduced pinprick + normal strength, vibration and reflexes + normal pulses and B12 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Drinks no alcohol**
whyNot.B: **B12 level is normal** and vibration sense is preserved
whyNot.C: **Both feet in a stocking pattern**, no back pain or reflex change
whyNot.D: **Strong pulses**, pain not exertional

why: **Long-standing diabetes with burning feet, allodynia and pinprick loss with normal vibration and reflexes** = diabetic neuropathy (small fibers affected first).

stem: A 63-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has foot pain that is worse at night and eases when she gets up and walks. Ankle reflexes are reduced, and pinprick and vibration are lost in a stocking pattern. Foot pulses are normal and the skin is warm and hairy. Hemoglobin and MCV are normal and she has no back pain.
oneliner: 63F + T2DM + night foot pain eased by walking + reduced ankle reflexes + stocking pinprick and vibration loss + normal pulses, Hb and MCV + no back pain → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Normal pulses and warm, hairy skin**
whyNot.C: **Hemoglobin and MCV are normal**, no spinal cord signs
